deep.reconstruction:
This folio contains no mathematical derivation. It holds three short reflective notes on mathematical method and pedagogy, separated by horizontal rules. They interrupt the surrounding research notes: the previous page treats a geometry-of-numbers / automorphic-function construction of a fundamental domain (Urbereich), and the next page continues the remark and then turns to reduced forms and a relative-abelian counterexample with K = Q(sqrt(-2), sqrt(-3)) over k = Q(sqrt 6).

(1) Oral tradition. Besides learning from books, learning through oral tradition now stands essentially on an equal footing. Hilbert gives himself as the example: he learned the whole Weierstrassian theory chiefly through Hurwitz.

(2) Why science does not choke on publication. So much is and has been published; why does science not suffocate from an overfull stomach? His answer is that ever sharper tools keep arising. These achieve what the earlier ones did and more, and so 'kill' the earlier ones. The pedagogical consequence: bring the sharp tools as early as possible, and do not let any regard for tradition (Ueberlieferung) deflect one from this principle.

(3) Mathematics and physics. It is often said that various mathematical disciplines first grew out of physics. One cannot conclude from this that these branches must still remain in constant connection with physics. This sentence continues onto the next page, with the image of a cutting (Ableger) that lets its link to the parent plant dry up once it has taken root. The continuation adds that mathematics is an independent, unified structure, and that one should avoid fragmenting oneself through too much stimulation and instead master the whole field.

There is nothing to compute or reconstruct in modern notation.

results.what: Remark that Hilbert learned the whole Weierstrassian theory mainly orally from Hurwitz.
results.usually_credited_to: Well documented: Hilbert's own obituary of Hurwitz (1920/21); Blumenthal's biography; Reid's 'Hilbert'

results.what: Thesis that sharper tools supersede and 'kill' older methods, which prevents science from being overwhelmed by publication; teach the sharp tools early.
results.modern_name: Hilbert's view of the progress and unity of mathematics (cf. the 1900 Paris lecture 'Mathematische Probleme')
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert, Paris ICM address 1900, which states essentially the same idea of sharper tools and simpler methods displacing older developments

results.what: Mathematics, though partly born from physics, need not remain tied to it (Ableger metaphor); mathematics is an autonomous, unified whole.
results.modern_name: Autonomy and unity of mathematics (Hilbert's methodological credo)
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert (1900 address; notebook remarks in Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600 discussed by Rowe, Corry and others)

deep.surprise_reason: These are personal methodological aphorisms consistent with Hilbert's published views, especially the 1900 Paris address on sharper tools and the unity of mathematics. His debt to Hurwitz is well documented. The wording is of mild archival interest, and the Ableger metaphor on mathematics' independence from physics is a nice quotable item. It contains no mathematical content and nothing that changes attribution.
